I’ve been farming these 6 mu in Quzhou for more than forty years, and I know this land like the backs of my hands. The soil is good, loamy yellow alluvial soil, and the climate here on the North China Plain is made for wheat and corn. I don’t gamble with new crops or fancy experiments—my father farmed wheat and corn, and this double-cropping system has put my own children through school. My winter wheat is already in the ground; we sowed it last October after the rains. Now it’s early spring, and the wheat is turning green, so my immediate work is top-dressing with urea, irrigating at the reviving-green stage, and then again at jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I’ll spray twice for aphids and powdery mildew—that’s usually enough. After the June harvest, I won’t rest more than a day; I’ll rotary-till the stubble and plant summer maize immediately to catch the heat. I use hybrid maize seed now because the county seed station has proven it gives 100–150 jin more per mu than the old open-pollinated types. For wheat, I stick with improved Jinmai varieties that handle our winters. Water is getting harder to pump—the groundwater table keeps dropping—so I irrigate four times for wheat and only twice for corn, just at the critical jointing and filling stages. I apply fertilizer based on what the soil testing van told me last year, rounded to what I can afford: about 22 kg nitrogen per mu for wheat and 19 kg for maize, plus some compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium.
